sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish copayments, deductibles, and coinsurance, and identify which cost-sharing type applies in a given scenario.
- Explain the out-of-pocket maximum and how copays, deductibles, and coinsurance accumulate toward it.
- Collect patient cost sharing at the front desk accurately and in accordance with office and payer policy.
- Explain patient responsibility clearly and respectfully, and escalate complex financial questions to authorized staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A copay is like a flat entrance fee at a movie: everyone pays the same small set price just to get the service, no matter what the visit costs.

### Question 2

A deductible is like the first part of a phone bill you must pay before a friend agrees to help split the rest.

### Question 3

Coinsurance is like splitting a restaurant bill by percentage: after the deductible, you pay your 20% slice and the plan pays the other 80%.

### Question 4

The out-of-pocket maximum is like a spending cap on a game: once you have paid up to that limit in a year, the plan covers the rest.

### Question 5

A copay is a set price tag, like a $3 toll, while coinsurance is a percentage split.

### Question 6

Coinsurance is like tipping a percentage of a bill, while a copay is a flat fee.

### Question 7

Cost sharing is the 'pay as you use it' part; the premium is the 'pay to keep the membership' part.

### Question 8

A $40 copay is like a $40 ticket at the door; you pay it when you walk in.

### Question 9

With 80/20, for every $10 of allowed cost the plan pays $8 and the patient pays $2.

### Question 10

A copay is collected at the door of the visit, like paying a toll as you drive through.

### Question 11

A deductible is like a yearly savings goal that starts back at zero every January.

### Question 12

Some checkups are like a free oil change: the plan covers them fully to keep you healthy.

### Question 13

Copays are like coins dropped in the yearly 'cap' jar, even if they do not fill up the separate deductible jar.

### Question 14

Coinsurance is the 'second stage' that starts only after you have filled the deductible bucket.

### Question 15

Once you fill the whole cap bucket, the plan takes over and pays the rest for covered care.

### Question 16

A family plan has a small 'per person' bucket and a bigger 'whole family' bucket.

### Question 17

An HDHP is like a cheaper monthly membership where you pay more of the first dollars yourself.

### Question 18

The assistant's job is to collect the set amount, like a cashier collecting a posted price, not to change it.

### Question 19

Checking eligibility is like checking a customer's membership card before ringing up a purchase.

### Question 20

Patient responsibility is the 'your share' line left after the insurance company pays its part.

### Question 21

A specialist visit often has a bigger 'door fee' than a regular checkup with your main doctor.

### Question 22

Coinsurance is figured on the 'agreed price,' not the sticker price.

### Question 23

Once the deductible bucket is full, you move to the 'split the rest by percentage' stage.

### Question 24

A copay is a fixed price tag on a service, like $1 per candy bar.

### Question 25

You check the price before you check out, so there are no surprises.

### Question 26

It is like explaining why you pay for your ticket before you enter the show.

### Question 27

You have $50 left to fill the deductible bucket before the plan starts helping.

### Question 28

Until the deductible bucket is full, you pay the full agreed price yourself.

### Question 29

When someone cannot pay at the door, you follow the rulebook and ask the manager rather than making up your own discount.

### Question 30

A copay is the patient's required share; quietly erasing it can break the rules with the insurance company.

### Question 31

After your deductible, you pay a slice of the pie and the plan pays the rest of the slices.

### Question 32

The EOB is the insurance company's 'here is what we did' note, not the doctor's bill.

### Question 33

Ring up the payment and hand over a receipt, just like a store cashier.

### Question 34

Money matters are private, like a secret you share quietly, not loudly in a crowd.

### Question 35

Keeping a card on file is like keeping a key: only with permission and kept safely locked up.

### Question 36

When a customer is upset about a price, you stay calm, follow the store's rules, and call a manager.

### Question 37

Check the price list for this customer's membership, not the person before them.

### Question 38

Your share is the total of your copay, deductible, and coinsurance pieces.

### Question 39

When the whole-family bucket is full, the plan starts helping everyone covered.

### Question 40

It is like each family member having their own small bucket inside the family's big bucket.

### Question 41

Copay coins fill the yearly cap jar, not the deductible jar.

### Question 42

Give your best estimate from the price sheet and say it is an estimate, not a promise.

### Question 43

Discounts need a manager's approval, not a cashier's guess.

### Question 44

It is like having two wallets: the first wallet pays, then the second may cover the leftover.

### Question 45

A video visit still has its posted price, just like an in-person one.

### Question 46

We check your insurance 'membership card' details to see your posted price.

### Question 47

Check the membership card every visit because benefits can change between visits.

### Question 48

Check the receipt history before deciding nothing more is owed.

### Question 49

Look at the paperwork together to see if the charge should really still be there.

### Question 50

A store may have a special sale, but only the manager sets it, not each cashier.

### Question 51

Check the receipt math with the correct price and percentage to be sure it adds up.

### Question 52

You can explain what the piggy bank is for, but an expert helps decide how to use it.

### Question 53

Filling the deductible bucket starts the percentage-split stage, which runs until the big cap is full.

### Question 54

When someone asks for help with a bill, you point them to the person who is allowed to say yes.

### Question 55

Keep the receipt and write it in the ledger so everyone knows it was paid.

### Question 56

Check the permission slip is signed before the big event, so there is no surprise bill.

### Question 57

If someone worries they cannot afford a repair, you point them to help, not tell them to skip it.

### Question 58

Use the agreed price ($300), not the sticker price ($500): 20% of $300 is $60.

### Question 59

Look up the posted price and tell the customer before they arrive.

### Question 60

When a bill feels big, a kind explanation and a helpful next step beats an argument.

### Question 61

If the membership card will not scan, you tell the customer and follow the store's backup plan.

### Question 62

The price on the tag is set by the plan, and the cashier collects what the tag says.

### Question 63

The cap bucket only counts for doctors in the plan's network; outside the network is a different rule.

### Question 64

If the store says this checkup is free under your plan, you do not charge for it.

### Question 65

If the receipt shows a double charge, tell the manager so it can be fixed.

### Question 66

Your percentage payments fill the yearly cap jar.

### Question 67

Once you hit the yearly cap, the plan covers the rest of the covered care until the year resets.

### Question 68

Three visits at $25 each: 25 plus 25 plus 25 equals 75.

### Question 69

Fill the last $400 of the bucket, then pay 20% of the leftover $200 ($40): total $440.

### Question 70

You are $150 away from the cap, so you pay just that last $150 and the plan covers the rest.

### Question 71

When your personal cap bucket is full, the plan covers your covered care even if the family bucket is not full yet.

### Question 72

You can explain how the puzzle pieces work, but an expert helps pick which puzzle to buy.

### Question 73

If a customer cannot afford their important medicine, you connect them to someone who can help, not say 'just stop.'

### Question 74

When a customer says a bill is wrong, you check it and hand it to the manager, not argue or delete it.

### Question 75

Fill the deductible bucket, then split by percentage, until the big cap stops the sharing.

### Question 76

The sticker price is not your price; your price is the agreed amount the plan uses.

### Question 77

Follow the store's rule: collect at the door, not later or never.

### Question 78

You can explain how the game works, but the coach makes the big strategy calls.

### Question 79

You can show your own price tag, but you cannot truthfully read another store's price tag for them.

### Question 80

If the plan says 'after the deductible, no more sharing,' then once that bucket is full your covered care is paid.

### Question 81

If a big bill is making someone want to stop their needed care, connect them to the helper, not say 'go ahead.'

### Question 82

Ask the official system for today's number, not a guess or an old note.

### Question 83

If the system says your share is zero today, the cashier takes zero.

### Question 84

The deductible bucket is already full when coinsurance starts, so the extra payments fill the cap jar instead.

### Question 85

You never write a fake number in the ledger; write what really happened and tell the manager.
